files.lesson.md: --- order: 10 unit: reals9 node: AC9M9N01 n1 uses: [AC9M8N01 n1, AC9M8N01 n2] assumes: [AC9M8N01 n1, AC9M8N01 n2] title: Number families summary: "Natural numbers sit inside the integers, the integers inside the rational numbers, and the rational and irrational numbers together make the real numbers. Each family was invented to answer a question the last couldn't." language: maths voice: { name: af_heart, speed: 1.1 } hook: "Each kind of number was invented because the old ones couldn't answer a question. Which question did each one answer?" --- You've met whole numbers, negatives, fractions and numbers like √2. They fit inside each other like nested boxes. ## Predict: the smallest family ```step stage: predict insight: "Committing to the smallest family before sorting shows who thinks the nesting stops at the rationals, or forgets √2 isn't a fraction." check: type: predict q: "Which is the smallest family that contains all of these: $7$, $-3$, $0.5$ and $\\sqrt{2}$?" options: - "The real numbers" - "The rational numbers" - "The integers" - "The natural numbers" actual: "The real numbers. 7 is natural, −3 is an integer, 0.5 = 1/2 is rational, but √2 never ends or repeats, so it's irrational. Rational and irrational numbers together make the real numbers." ``` Four questions, and each needs a bigger kind of number. Which family holds a number that answers all four? ## Run: sort the numbers ```step stage: run insight: "Sorting numbers into their smallest family shows the nesting: a number can belong to several families, but has one smallest." check: type: sort q: "Which is the smallest family that each number belongs to?" options: ["Natural", "Integer", "Rational", "Irrational"] items: - ["5", "Natural"] - ["−2", "Integer", "It's a whole number, but below the naturals."] - ["3/4", "Rational"] - ["√7", "Irrational"] - ["√16", "Natural", "√16 = 4."] - ["−√9", "Integer", "−√9 = −3."] - ["0.333…", "Rational", "It's 1/3."] - ["π", "Irrational"] explain: "Each number goes in the smallest family that holds it. 5 is also an integer and rational, but its smallest family is natural." ``` Natural numbers are 1, 2, 3 and so on. Integers add zero and the negatives. Rational numbers can be written as a fraction of two integers. Irrational numbers can't. ## Investigate: the nesting ```step stage: investigate insight: "Every natural number is an integer, every integer is rational and every rational is real. Having a root sign doesn't make a number irrational: it depends on what's under it. Zoe judges √16 by the sign." tasks: - check: type: question q: "True or false: every integer is a rational number." options: ["True: 5 = 5/1", "False: integers aren't fractions", "False: only positive integers are", "It depends on the integer"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Any integer can be written as a fraction with 1 underneath.", "−5 = −5/1 is also rational.", "Every integer can be written over 1."] explain: "Any integer n is the fraction n/1, so every integer is rational." - check: type: bug code: "working.txt#zoe" text: "Zoe decides whether √16 is rational or irrational. Click the line where her thinking goes wrong." answer: 2 fault: logic misconception: root-sign-irrational explain: "Line 2: a root sign doesn't make a number irrational. √16 = 4, a whole number, so it's rational. √7 would be irrational: 7 isn't a perfect square." - check: type: number q: "How many of $\\sqrt{4}$, $\\sqrt{5}$, $\\sqrt{9}$, $\\sqrt{10}$ and $\\sqrt{16}$ are irrational?" answer: 2 explain: "√4 = 2, √9 = 3 and √16 = 4 are whole numbers. √5 and √10 are irrational." ``` ### Every integer The nesting, step by step. ```worked 5 :: Natural: a counting number. -5 :: Not natural. Integer. -5 = \tfrac{-5}{1} :: So it's also rational. \tfrac{1}{2} :: Rational, not an integer. \sqrt{2} :: Not a fraction: irrational. \text{rational} + \text{irrational} = \text{real} :: Every number on the number line is real. ``` Now try one on paper: for each of $\sqrt{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$, $-3$, $\sqrt{3}$ and $5$, write whether it's rational. Then type how many are. ### Find the mistake Read Zoe's thinking. What decides if a root is irrational? ### Count the irrationals ## Modify: change the number ```step stage: modify insight: "Changing one number at a time: a root of a perfect square, an irrational plus its opposite, and a decimal that stops." tasks: - hint: ["Is 25 a perfect square?", "5 × 5 = 25."] check: { type: question, q: "Is $\\sqrt{25}$ rational or irrational?", options: ["Rational: it equals 5", "Irrational: it has a root sign"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "A root sign doesn't make a number irrational: 5 × 5 = 25."], explain: "√25 = 5, a whole number." } smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "What number times itself makes 25?", answer: 5, explain: "5 × 5 = 25, so √25 = 5." } - hint: ["Work it out: √2 + (−√2).", "What is a number plus its opposite?"] check: { type: question, q: "Edge case: is $\\sqrt{2} + (-\\sqrt{2})$ rational or irrational?", options: ["Rational: it's 0", "Irrational: both parts are irrational"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "Two irrationals can add to a rational: the parts cancel."], explain: "√2 + (−√2) = 0, which is rational." } - hint: ["It stops. Can you write it as a fraction?", "0.125 = 125/1000."] check: { type: question, q: "Is $0.125$ rational or irrational?", options: ["Rational: it stops, so it's a fraction", "Irrational: it has a decimal point"], answer: 0, feedback: [null, "A decimal that stops is a fraction: 125/1000 = 1/8."], explain: "0.125 = 125/1000 = 1/8." } ``` ### A root of a square ### Two irrationals ### A short decimal ## Practise: which family ```step stage: practise insight: "Sorting again with new numbers; the review keeps exact and rounded values separate." tasks: - check: type: sort q: "Which is the smallest family that each number belongs to?" options: ["Natural", "Integer", "Rational", "Irrational"] items: - ["12", "Natural"] - ["−8", "Integer"] - ["2/5", "Rational"] - ["√11", "Irrational"] - ["√49", "Natural", "√49 = 7."] - ["0.75", "Rational", "It's 3/4."] - ["−1.5", "Rational", "It's −3/2."] explain: "Perfect-square roots are whole numbers, stopping decimals are fractions, and √ of a non-square never ends or repeats." - check: type: question q: "Which is irrational?" options: ["$\\sqrt{12}$", "$\\sqrt{36}$", "$\\tfrac{22}{7}$", "$0.\\overline{3}$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "√36 = 6.", "22/7 is a fraction, so it's rational (it's only close to π).", "0.333… is 1/3."] explain: "12 isn't a perfect square, so √12 never ends or repeats." smaller: check: { type: "number", q: "Which whole number squared is closest below 12? Type it.", answer: 3, explain: "3² = 9 and 4² = 16, so 12 is between them: not a perfect square." } - check: type: question q: "True or false: the real numbers include both rational and irrational numbers." options: ["True", "False: they're only the irrationals", "False: they're only the rationals"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "Rational numbers are real too.", "Irrational numbers are real too."] explain: "Every point on the number line is a real number." - check: type: number q: "Review: what's the exact value of $\\sqrt{81}$?" answer: 9 explain: "9 × 9 = 81." ``` ### Sort again ### Spot the irrational ### The real numbers ### Review A square root, from Irrational numbers. ## Make: why each family exists ```step stage: make insight: "Coming back to the opening: each equation needs a family, and the smallest one that holds the answer shows why it was invented." tasks: - hint: ["Solve each equation.", "Then ask: is the answer a whole number, a fraction, or neither?"] check: type: reasoning paper: true q: "Solve $x + 5 = 2$, $3x = 2$, $x^2 = 2$ and $x^2 = 9$ (positive answers for the squares). How many of the four answers are NOT rational?" steps: - ["$x = -3$", "an integer, so also rational"] - ["$x = \\tfrac{2}{3}$", "rational"] - ["$x = \\sqrt{2}$", "irrational: 2 isn't a perfect square"] - ["$x = 3$", "natural, so also rational"] answer: "1" answerLabel: "Answers that are not rational" feedback: - ["0", "x² = 2 has the answer √2, which is irrational."] - ["2", "Only x² = 2 is not rational: x² = 9 gives 3."] criteria: - "I solved each equation before sorting." - "I remembered that √9 = 3 is a whole number." - "My answer is the number of irrational solutions." explain: "−3, 2/3 and 3 are rational. Only √2 is irrational." - check: type: question q: "Which equation first needed negative numbers?" options: ["$x + 5 = 2$", "$3x = 2$", "$x^2 = 2$"] answer: 0 feedback: [null, "3x = 2 gave a fraction, 2/3.", "x² = 2 gave an irrational number."] explain: "x = −3: the integers were invented to answer questions like this." ``` ### Who's not rational? Back to the four questions. Work these out on paper first, then type your answer. ### The first negative **Also used in** - **Everyday numbers.** Counting uses naturals, money and temperatures use integers and rationals, and measuring a diagonal can need an irrational. - **Next lesson.** Exact values like √2 and rounded ones like 1.41: when each is needed. ```teacher summary: Students sort numbers into natural, integer, rational and irrational, see why the families nest inside each other, and learn that a root sign alone doesn't make a number irrational (AC9M9N01, node 1). time: 35 timing: Predict and Run 8 min · Investigate 10 min · Modify 8 min · Practise and Make 9 min goals: - I can say which families a number belongs to. - I can explain why every integer is rational. - I can tell √16 from √7. struggle: "Deciding about roots. Ask: is the number under the root a perfect square?" before: > Students need Irrational numbers and Recurring decimals from Year 8. The one idea: the families nest. A number belongs to several, but has one smallest. The common mistake is calling any root irrational (Zoe's thinking). Natural numbers: here counting numbers 1, 2, 3, ... Say if your school includes 0. running: - "Predict: take a show of hands. Those who chose the rationals forgot √2 isn't a fraction." - "Run: ask for the smallest family, not any family." - "Paper: the try-one after the worked example and the four equations in Make are worked on paper first. Books out, and look for each answer written out before it's sorted." - "Modify: before √2 + (−√2), ask what a number plus its opposite is." stuck: - see: A student calls √16 irrational. ask: What is √16? fix: "4: a whole number, so rational." - see: A student says 0.5 isn't rational because it has a decimal point. ask: Can you write 0.5 as a fraction? fix: "1/2: rational." stretch: Is the sum of two irrational numbers always irrational? Is the product? support: "A set of nested boxes: natural, integer, rational, real, with irrational outside the rationals." leads: > Starts AC9M9N01. Where it leads: exact or rounded (next), intervals on the number line, formulas with π and roots. exit: q: Is √20 rational or irrational? Why? a: "Irrational: 20 isn't a perfect square." explain: > The natural numbers are inside the integers, the integers are inside the rational numbers, and the rational and irrational numbers together are the real numbers. Each family answers a question the last couldn't: $2 - 5$ needs negatives, $1 \div 2$ needs fractions, and $x^2 = 2$ needs irrationals. ```
